uncertainty_flags: No confidence intervals or statistical tests reported for accuracy gains.
Comparisons to prior work may be confounded by differing speaker-split protocols and preprocessing (e.g., translation of MOUD).
Hierarchical advantage may be conflated with staged training instead of architecture alone.
bc-LSTM results rely on offline access to future utterances; applicability to online settings is unclear.
Feature-extraction choices (word2vec, 3D-CNN design, openSMILE config) might drive part of the improvements.
alternative_interpretations: Reported accuracy gains stem primarily from improved unimodal features (text-CNN, 3D-CNN architecture, openSMILE config) rather than contextual LSTM modeling.
Hierarchical fusion gains result from staged optimization and extra parameter tuning rather than an inherent representational benefit of hierarchical architecture.
bc-LSTM benefits reflect access to future labels/utterances (data leakage in offline evaluation) rather than superior modeling of causal context.

Cross-lingual robustness of visual features in MOSI→MOUD may reflect language-induced token mismatch hurting textual models artificially (translation/embedding mismatch), not a fundamental superiority of visual modality.
transparency_notes: Code and full hyperparameter configurations are not provided in the manuscript; this limits reproducibility.
Single-split experiments and lack of variance reporting reduce transparency about result stability.
Details of masking/padding and batching during LSTM training are not fully specified.
Comparison with prior SOTA does not control for speaker-split differences, which should be clearly annotated when reporting relative gains.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The hierarchical-contextual framing (train unimodal contextual sequence models, then fuse their contextual outputs with another contextual sequence model) appears to be a novel architectural framing relative to the cited baselines; this novelty is orthogonal to the empirical validity of reported gains — novelty should be preserved and tested, not penalized merely because close analogs are sparse.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If unimodal features are held constant and hierarchical fusion still improves accuracy across multiple random speaker-disjoint folds with statistically significant margins, the framing is validated.

If joint end-to-end training fails to match staged hierarchical training but staged training generalizes better to new speakers, the hierarchical training regimen (not just architecture) may be the key operational insight.

If bc-LSTM advantages vanish in causal/online evaluation (no future context), the conceptual contribution is constrained to offline/video-level analysis; conversely, if offline gains translate into better downstream summary analysis, the approach is impactful in archival/video analytics.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The combination of (a) creating context-aware unimodal representations via sequence models, (b) then fusing those context-aware unimodal streams via a second-level contextual sequence model (hierarchical contextual fusion), and (c) empirically exploring architectural variants (sc/h/bc-LSTM) constitutes a coherent conceptual frame that is not well represented in the cited prior art and may open new directions in multimodal temporal fusion.
evidence: Section 3.3.2 describes hierarchical two-level architecture and Algorithm 1 details successive training.
Retrieved literature and references (Poria et al., Rozgic et al.) do not appear to propose the exact hierarchical contextual stacking.
uncertainty_flags: Innovation signal present but requires stronger isolating experiments to demonstrate that hierarchy (not training regimen or features) is the causal factor for gains.

novelty_lenses.verdict: partially incremental relative to sequence-modeling literature
novelty_lenses.rationale: Sequence modeling for emotion/sentiment has precedent (Wöllmer et al. and others). From this perspective, applying LSTMs to utterance sequences and demonstrating gains is an extension rather than a paradigm shift; the hierarchical fusion proposal is the main differentiator.
evidence: Wöllmer et al. advocate for long-range dependency modeling; prior SOTA used feature fusion and kernel approaches.
Paper evaluates known variants (bidirectional vs unidirectional) and reports expected bc-LSTM gains.
uncertainty_flags: Distinguishing true novelty from well-executed incremental improvement depends on controlled ablations and broader validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects (a) high confidence in identified methodological gaps (statistical reporting, training regimen confounds, translation effects) and (b) moderate-to-high confidence that the conceptual hierarchical-contextual framing is an innovation signal. Uncertainty remains about how much of reported empirical gains are attributable to contextual modeling versus preprocessing/training choices; resolving this requires additional experiments.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes applying contextual LSTMs at the utterance sequence level for multimodal (text, audio, visual) utterance-level sentiment/emotion classification, compares three LSTM variants (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) and two fusion strategies (non-hierarchical vs hierarchical where unimodal contextual LSTMs are trained then fused). Reported empirical results (Tables 4–6) show consistent accuracy gains over a uni-SVM baseline and cited prior work on MOSI, MOUD and IEMOCAP under speaker-independent splits, with stated overall improvements of ~5–10% over prior SOTA and 2–5% vs uni-SVM. Evidence in the manuscript supports that context modeling helps (improvements across datasets and modalities), bc-LSTM often outperforms unidirectional variants, and hierarchical fusion generally beats non-hierarchical fusion. However, critical experimental controls are missing: no confidence intervals, no multiple-split/fold variance, hierarchical training is staged (not joint) which may conflate training-regime with architecture, and MOUD textual preprocessing (Google Translate) and feature choices (word2vec, openSMILE, 3D-CNN) can confound comparisons to prior work. The cross-dataset MOSI→MOUD experiment suggests visual features are more robust cross-lingually, but translation/noise and single transfer direction limit generality. Overall, the core claim that temporal contextual LSTM modeling improves utterance-level multimodal classification is supported by the presented within-protocol results, but the magnitude and generality of the gains are uncertain due to the methodological omissions and confounds noted below.
logical_argument_graph: A1 (utterances in a video are correlated) -> motivates contextual modeling with LSTM
Context-independent unimodal features (text-CNN, openSMILE, 3D-CNN) -> inputs to contextual LSTM
Contextual LSTM variants (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) -> produce context-dependent utterance features
Fusion strategies: non-hierarchical (concat raw features) vs hierarchical (concat unimodal contextual outputs) -> Level-2 LSTM classifies fused features
Empirical evaluation on MOSI/MOUD/IEMOCAP with speaker-disjoint splits -> Tables 4–6 report accuracies
Observed: contextual LSTMs > uni-SVM, bc-LSTM > sc/h-LSTM, hierarchical > non-hierarchical, text typically strongest unimodal
Caveats: single-split evaluation, lack of statistical tests, MOUD translation confound, staged hierarchical training confound
Conclusion: context modeling plausibly beneficial; effect sizes and generalizability require further controlled experiments

identified_claims.claim_text: An LSTM-based framework that models inter-utterance dependencies yields substantial improvements (reported 5–10% over prior work) for utterance-level multimodal sentiment and emotion recognition.
evidence: Abstract: 'Our model shows 5 − 10% improvement over the state of the art.'
Section 4.2: Tables 4 and 5 show contextual LSTM variants outperform uni-SVM and reported state-of-the-art numbers.
uncertainty_flags: No confidence intervals or multiple runs reported; single-split point estimates only.
The 5–10% claim mixes within-paper comparisons and comparisons to prior work that used different speaker-split protocols (possible unfairness).
Improvement magnitude varies by dataset (IEMOCAP shows larger gains), so the 5–10% is dataset-dependent and not uniformly substantiated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Hierarchical fusion—training unimodal contextual LSTMs per modality and then fusing their outputs with another contextual LSTM—outperforms non-hierarchical fusion and simple concatenation.
evidence: Section 3.3.2 describes the hierarchical two-level scheme.
Section 4.2 and Table 4 show hierarchical framework yields higher accuracies than non-hierarchical variants (reported for bc-LSTM and others).
uncertainty_flags: Level-1 and Level-2 are trained successively and separately; gains may partly reflect staged training/hyperparameter differences rather than inherent architecture advantage.
Numerical margins are shown but no statistical testing or repeated folds to confirm consistency.

identified_claims.claim_text: Bi-directional contextual LSTM (bc-LSTM) generally outperforms unidirectional variants because it can use both preceding and following utterances.
evidence: Architectural description of bc-LSTM as bidirectional.
Section 4.2: statement 'bc-LSTM ... performs consistently better on all the datasets over sc-LSTM' and tables with higher bc-LSTM accuracies.
uncertainty_flags: bc-LSTM requires access to future context—valid in offline/video-level evaluation but not in causal/online settings; claim implicitly assumes offline availability.
Numerical improvements are dataset-dependent and modest in some cases; no variance reported.

identified_claims.claim_label: contextual models beat uni-SVM and prior SOTA
identified_claims.claim_text: Contextual models outperform a baseline unimodal-SVM and prior state-of-the-art methods (e.g., Poria et al., 2015; Rozgic et al., 2012b) on benchmark datasets (MOSI, MOUD, IEMOCAP) under speaker-independent splits.
evidence: Tables 4–5 show LSTM variants surpass uni-SVM by ~2–5% in reported experiments.
Table 5 lists higher accuracy numbers than the cited Poria et al. (2015) and Rozgic et al. (2012b) entries.
uncertainty_flags: Prior works used speaker-overlapping splits—authors note this but do not re-run prior methods under speaker-disjoint splits, so comparisons may not be apples-to-apples.
MOUD results use Google-translated transcripts to match prior English-based setups; translation approach and its noise complicate fairness of comparisons.

identified_claims.claim_text: Modalities contribute unevenly: text often provides the strongest unimodal signal, audio stronger than visual overall, but visual modality shows more robustness in cross-lingual transfer.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'textual classifier achieves the best performance' and 'audio modality has performed better than visual on all the datasets.'
Section 4.4 and Table 6: MOSI→MOUD transfer shows visual modality fares better than text/audio.
uncertainty_flags: MOUD textual underperformance depends on translation; Spanish word vectors improved text by ~10% when tested, so modality ranking is sensitive to preprocessing.
Ranking varies by dataset and margins are sometimes small; single-split results only.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed contextual approach improves generalization in speaker-independent settings.
evidence: Authors use speaker-disjoint splits for train/test and show contextual LSTM gains under those splits versus uni-SVM.
Section 4.1 justification of speaker-independent evaluation to emulate unseen conditions.
uncertainty_flags: No direct comparison to speaker-dependent splits to quantify generalization gap; single speaker-split per dataset reduces confidence about robustness across different speaker partitions.
Potential confound: larger model capacity of LSTMs vs. SVM might explain some gains, not only contextual modeling.

identified_claims.claim_text: Cross-dataset/language transfer (MOSI→MOUD) shows modality-dependent degradation: audio and text degrade substantially while visual is more robust.
evidence: Table 6 MOSI→MOUD: T and A accuracies are low; V relatively higher.
Section 4.4 textual explanation attributes poor T/A performance to language mismatch.
uncertainty_flags: MOUD transcripts were machine-translated; translation noise confounds modality comparison. Authors acknowledge Spanish-word-vector experiment improves text substantially.
Only MOSI→MOUD direction tested; not shown whether visual robustness generalizes to other dataset pairs or languages.

identified_claims.claim_text: Including a dense layer after LSTM (as in sc-LSTM and bc-LSTM) improves performance over the variant without the dense layer (h-LSTM), with improvements reported between 0.3%–1.5% on MOSI/MOUD and 1%–5% on IEMOCAP.
evidence: Section 3.2.3 defines h-LSTM (no dense) and sc-LSTM (with dense).
Section 4.2 reports the performance improvement ranges and Table 4 shows per-dataset numbers.
uncertainty_flags: Reported gains for dense-layer variants are small in some cases (sub-1%); without run-to-run variance these may be within noise.
The effect of dense layer might interact with other hyperparameters (dropout, hidden size) not fully controlled or reported.

strengths.title: Clear motivation for temporal context
strengths.description: The manuscript motivates modeling inter-utterance dependencies with concrete examples and theoretical justification (utterances in a video are often correlated).
evidence: Introduction example from MOSI demonstrating context disambiguation.
Section 3.2 rationale: 'there is a high probability of utterance relatedness...'

strengths.title: Well-specified architectures and ablation
strengths.description: Authors provide explicit descriptions of multiple LSTM variants (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) and both hierarchical and non-hierarchical fusion pipelines enabling reproducibility of the architectural choices.
evidence: Section 3.2.3 details LSTM variants and training.
Algorithm 1 and Table 2 summarize procedural steps and parameters.

strengths.title: Evaluation on multiple public benchmarks with speaker-disjoint splits
strengths.description: Paper reports experiments on MOSI, MOUD, and IEMOCAP using speaker-independent splits to test generalization to unseen speakers.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes speaker-disjoint splits and Table 3 split details.
Results across three datasets presented in Tables 4–6.

concerns.title: Lack of statistical significance and variance reporting
concerns.description: Experimental results are presented as single-point accuracies without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or multiple speaker-split runs; small reported gains (often <2–3%) could be unstable.
evidence: No mention of multiple runs, cross-validation, or CI in Sections 4.2–4.4; tables list point accuracies only.
Prior-stage reviewers highlight absence of variance and statistical testing in shared analysis.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run each key experiment across multiple random speaker-disjoint splits (or k-fold speaker-level CV), report mean ± std and perform statistical tests (e.g., paired bootstrap or McNemar) to establish significance of reported gains.

concerns.title: Confound between hierarchical fusion and staged training regime
concerns.description: Hierarchical fusion trains Level-1 unimodal LSTMs separately then Level-2, which may benefit from different hyperparameter selection or representational capacity rather than the architecture itself.
evidence: Section 3.3.2: 'we train Level 1 and Level 2 successively but separately.'
Shared analysis notes potential confound between staged training and architecture.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a joint end-to-end trained hierarchical baseline (same architecture but trained jointly) and control for hyperparameters to isolate whether staged training or the hierarchical structure yields gains.

concerns.title: Preprocessing and feature-extraction confounds
concerns.description: Comparisons to prior work and modality rankings depend on specific feature pipelines (word2vec trained on Google News, openSMILE config, 3D-CNN choices) and MOUD translation; these choices can drive performance differences.
evidence: Section 3.1 describes textual features using GoogleNews word2vec and a two-layer CNN; audio uses openSMILE 6373 features; visual uses 3D-CNN with specified filter sizes.
Section 4.3 notes Spanish word vectors improve MOUD text by ~10% relative to translated transcripts.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablations showing sensitivity of results to key preprocessing: (a) replace Google News word2vec with in-language embeddings (Spanish) for MOUD or show results both ways; (b) document openSMILE config and 3D-CNN training details; (c) re-run prior baselines with identical preprocessing where possible.

concerns.title: Bi-directional LSTM applicability limited to offline settings
concerns.description: bc-LSTM uses future utterances and therefore the reported gains do not translate to real-time/streaming applications where future context is not available.
evidence: Section 3.2.3 defines bc-LSTM as using preceding and following utterances; no online/causal variant evaluated.
Shared analysis flags bc-LSTM assumption of full-video availability.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify intended deployment setting; include experiments comparing bc-LSTM (offline) to causal variants (e.g., sc-LSTM with larger history or attention) and report trade-offs.

concerns.title: Cross-dataset transfer experiment limited and confounded
concerns.description: MOSI→MOUD transfer uses machine-translated transcripts and only one transfer direction; conclusions about modality robustness (visual superiority) may be driven by translation noise rather than inherent robustness.
evidence: Section 4.4: MOSI→MOUD uses Google Translate for MOUD and authors note translation noise; Table 6 shows V outperforming T/A.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers note limitation of single direction and translation confound.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add experiments with native-language embeddings (Spanish) and/or evaluate MOUD→MOSI transfer if possible; report results with human-verified transcripts or both translated and native embeddings to disentangle translation effects.

concerns.title: Evaluation metric choice and class imbalance
concerns.description: Paper reports accuracy only; for multiclass IEMOCAP and datasets with class imbalance, accuracy may misrepresent performance (no F1, per-class recall).
evidence: Tables 4–6 report only accuracy percentages; Section 4.2/4.3 discussions center on accuracy.
IEMOCAP includes multiple emotion classes and authors note poor neutral classification.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-class precision/recall/F1, macro- and micro-F1 or balanced accuracy for datasets with imbalance to provide a fuller picture of performance.

comparable_works.relevance: Primary prior SOTA compared in paper (multimodal utterance-level sentiment using text-CNN + MKL).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar use of textual CNNs and multimodal features but prior work used MKL/SVM fusion and did not use speaker-independent splits or explicit inter-utterance sequence modeling with LSTMs.
comparable_works.source_trace: MANUSCRIPT references and Table 5 comparison; Poria et al. 2015 citation in manuscript.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior SOTA for multimodal emotion recognition used ensemble SVM trees; compared in paper for IEMOCAP.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Feature-level fusion and SVM-tree ensembles; lacks sequential/contextual LSTM modeling used here.
comparable_works.source_trace: MANUSCRIPT references and Table 5 comparison; Rozgic et al. 2012b citation.

comparable_works.relevance: Work on continuous emotion recognition and multimodal sentiment in videos that motivated sequential modeling.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Wöllmer et al. used sequential models for continuous emotion recognition; the present paper adapts LSTM to utterance-level multimodal classification, building on that motivation.
comparable_works.source_trace: MANUSCRIPT references (Wöllmer et al. 2013, Wöllmer et al. 2008) and Section 4.2 discussion.

comparable_works.relevance: General multimodal fusion literature—discusses early vs late fusion strategies and hierarchical fusion variants as context.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Addresses fusion taxonomy; not specific to temporal utterance sequences but conceptually relevant for fusion choices.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature: multimodal fusion overview in top documents.

uncertainty_flags: No reported confidence intervals / standard deviations or multiple-split variability for reported accuracies.
Comparisons to prior SOTA may be unfair due to differing speaker-split protocols (speaker-overlap vs speaker-disjoint) and preprocessing differences (MOUD translation).
Hierarchical fusion gains may be confounded with staged (successive) training rather than architecture alone.
bc-LSTM results assume offline access to future utterances; not applicable to online/streaming use-cases.
Cross-dataset MOSI→MOUD conclusions limited by single transfer direction and translation noise.
alternative_interpretations: Reported gains could be partially attributed to improved feature extraction (text-CNN, 3D-CNN, openSMILE parameterization) rather than context modeling alone—if feature pipelines differ from prior work, gains may reflect preprocessing improvements.

Staged hierarchical training might act as a form of representation specialization or implicit regularization; hierarchical > non-hierarchical gains may reflect training dynamics rather than inherent structural advantage.

The apparent robustness of visual features in MOSI→MOUD could stem from translation noise harming text and audio models or from domain mismatches (recording conditions), not intrinsic transferability of facial features.

bc-LSTM gains may exploit future context that correlates strongly with labels in these datasets (e.g., monotonic sentiment across a video); such datasets favor offline bidirectional methods and results may overstate benefits for real-time applications.
transparency_notes: Key hyperparameters and preprocessing choices are described (word2vec Google News, CNN kernel sizes, openSMILE feature count, 3D-CNN filter sizes), but full training hyperparameters (LSTM hidden sizes, learning rates, number of epochs, early stopping criteria) and open-source code/seed values are not provided—this hinders reproducibility.

Hierarchical training is done successively but exact validation/hyperparameter selection procedures for Level-1 vs Level-2 are not fully specified; reporting these would improve reproducibility and clarity.

MOUD transcripts were machine-translated with Google Translate; authors also note Spanish word vectors improve performance, but main reported numbers use translated transcripts to match prior work—this choice should be clearly flagged in tables as a confound when comparing cross-lingual results.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The hierarchical contextual LSTM framing and systematic ablation over LSTM variants and fusion strategies appears to lack an exact close precedent in the retrieved corpus, which suggests genuine novelty; however, novelty alone does not validate empirical claims—robust methodological controls and statistical evidence are still required to confirm the reported gains.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If results hold with multiple speaker-disjoint splits and the mean improvement remains significantly positive, the architecture likely provides consistent gains.
If the hierarchical gain persists when trained end-to-end (joint optimization) rather than staged, that supports architectural benefit rather than staged-training artifacts.
If replacing translated MOUD transcripts with native-language embeddings preserves cross-dataset visual robustness, then the visual modality claim is more credible.

If bc-LSTM advantage persists when comparing to stronger unidirectional causal models (e.g., sc-LSTM with attention over longer history), the bidirectional benefit is substantive beyond offline-only artifacts.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying LSTMs to model utterance-level temporal context and systematically comparing hierarchical fusion and LSTM variants is a meaningful extension of prior multimodal fusion work; similar ideas (sequential modeling) exist in the literature but the specific hierarchical-contextual pipeline is not extensively documented in cited works.
evidence: Prior SOTA (Poria et al., 2015; Rozgic et al., 2012b) used MKL/SVM-tree fusion without inter-utterance LSTM modeling; Wöllmer et al. used sequential modeling for continuous tasks, but not this exact utterance-level hierarchical fusion.
uncertainty_flags: Potential novelty risk from insufficient control experiments (e.g., staged training confound) that could explain gains rather than novel architecture per se.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Framing utterance-level multimodal fusion as hierarchical contextual sequence modeling could shift how multimodal signals are aggregated over time, but to be considered disruptive it requires stronger empirical isolation (robust cross-dataset gains, ablation vs joint training) and broader demonstration beyond the three datasets.
evidence: Authors present hierarchical contextual fusion with Level-1 unimodal LSTMs feeding Level-2; this two-level fusion with temporal modeling per modality is not common in the cited prior work.
uncertainty_flags: No end-to-end joint-training baseline and limited generalization experiments reduce confidence in disruptive impact.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (lower bound ~0.4) that the core qualitative claim (temporal/contextual LSTM modeling can help utterance-level multimodal sentiment/emotion classification) is supported by the paper's within-protocol results; confidence is limited (upper bound ~0.85) because the main quantitative claims (magnitude 5–10% and cross-dataset generality) lack statistical validation, multiple-split robustness checks, and control for preprocessing/training confounds.

consensus_findings: Modeling temporal context across utterances with LSTM-based architectures plausibly improves utterance-level multimodal sentiment/emotion classification in the offline (full-video) setting: multiple reviewers observed consistent within-protocol accuracy gains of the proposed contextual LSTM variants versus a uni-SVM baseline on MOSI, MOUD and IEMOCAP.

Hierarchical fusion (training unimodal contextual LSTMs then fusing their contextual outputs with a second-level contextual LSTM) is a coherent architectural proposal and shows reported empirical gains relative to a non-hierarchical concatenation-then-LSTM pipeline in the manuscript's experiments.
Bi-directional contextual LSTM (bc-LSTM) tends to outperform unidirectional variants in the reported offline experiments where future utterances are available at test time.

Textual features generally provide the strongest unimodal signal in-language, with audio often stronger than visual on the in-language datasets; visual features showed relatively higher robustness in the single reported cross-dataset (MOSI→MOUD) experiment.

The manuscript documents architectures and experimental procedures clearly enough to enable targeted reproduction attempts in principle (pseudocode, feature extractor descriptions, and variant definitions are present).
disagreements: Magnitude and generality of the reported 5–10% 'state-of-the-art' improvement: some reviewers interpret the numbers as promising but provisional due to single-split reporting and potential preprocessing differences (translation, embeddings), while others emphasize that without re-running prior methods under the same speaker-disjoint protocol the cross-paper SOTA claim is not directly comparable.

Source of gains for hierarchical fusion: one interpretation is that the hierarchical architectural inductive bias yields better multimodal contextual representations; an alternate interpretation is that staged (separate) training, per-modality hyperparameter tuning, or increased effective parameter/optimization budget produced the observed advantage. Reviewers disagree about how strongly the paper rules out the latter.

Role of feature/extraction choices vs contextual modeling: some reviewers view contextual LSTMs as the main driver of improvements; others consider that stronger unimodal preprocessing (text-CNN, 3D-CNN, openSMILE configuration, embedding choices) could explain a substantial portion of reported gains.

Novelty framing: reviewers differ on whether the hierarchical contextual stacking is a modest incremental composition of known modules (majority view) or a meaningful conceptual innovation that opens new directions (minority disruptive-leaning view).
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical robustness: no reported confidence intervals, no multi-fold speaker-disjoint cross-validation or repeated runs; small reported margins (often <2–5%) may be within experimental noise.

Fairness of SOTA comparisons: prior cited baselines often used different speaker-split protocols (speaker-overlapping) and the paper does not re-evaluate those baselines under the same speaker-disjoint splits, confounding cross-paper claims.
Hierarchical fusion vs. staged-training confound: Level-1 and Level-2 are trained successively (not jointly); unclear whether architecture or training regimen explains gains.

MOUD textual preprocessing: use of Google Translate versus native-language embeddings (authors report Spanish embeddings can change results by ~10%) compromises modality comparisons and cross-lingual transfer conclusions.

bc-LSTM applicability: bi-directional models rely on future utterances and thus reported gains are limited to offline/whole-video scenarios; implications for online/streaming deployment are unresolved.

Implementation/operational details: masking/padding mechanics, exact optimizer hyperparameters, number of runs, random seeds, and openSMILE/3D-CNN configs are incompletely specified for full reproducibility.
model_diversity_effects: Architectural diversity (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) provided useful sensitivity analysis: reviewers agree bc-LSTM often achieved the highest offline accuracy, but magnitude varied by dataset and lacks variance estimates.

Fusion diversity (hierarchical vs non-hierarchical) revealed a potential benefit of per-modality contextual pretraining; however, model-diversity also highlighted a training-regime artifact risk because hierarchical models were trained in stages while the non-hierarchical baseline was not matched for training schedule or joint optimization.

Modality diversity surfaced dataset- and preprocessing-dependent modality rankings (text > audio > visual in-language; visual relatively stronger under MOSI→MOUD transfer). Reviewers note that this diversity is informative but sensitive to embedding and translation choices, implying modality-effect estimates depend on pipeline decisions.

Diverse reviewer roles (structure analyst, methodology auditor, novelty assessors) converged on the qualitative promise of context modeling but the methodological and reproducibility-focused reviewers emphasized uncertainty about quantitative generality—this role-induced diversity increases scrutiny of experimental controls and signals where additional experiments would be most informative.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center decision-making on whether the manuscript's empirical claims are sufficiently supported by robust, reproducible evidence. Critical experiments and reporting that would materially reduce uncertainty include: (1) running key experiments across multiple random speaker-disjoint splits (or k-fold speaker-level CV) and reporting mean ± std and appropriate statistical tests for pairwise comparisons (hierarchical vs non-hierarchical; bc-LSTM vs sc/h-LSTM); (2) providing an end-to-end joint-training baseline for the hierarchical architecture (or freezing/fine-tuning ablations) to disentangle staged-training effects from architectural benefits; (3) clarifying and, where possible, mitigating MOUD translation confounds by reporting results with native-language embeddings (Spanish) and/or both translated and native pipelines; (4) documenting full implementation details (masking/padding, optimizer hyperparameters, seeds, exact openSMILE configuration, 3D-CNN training regimen) or releasing code/data splits to enable independent reproduction. Ask authors to (a) mark comparisons to prior SOTA as not directly comparable when evaluation protocols differ, and (b) temper cross-dataset and SOTA magnitude claims until robustness checks are added. The editor should request these targeted reproducibility and control experiments before relying on the precise numerical claims for editorial decisions or broader claims about generality.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical claims and reduce interpretive uncertainty, please provide the following: (1) Multiple-run statistics: repeat key experiments across several randomized speaker-disjoint splits (or speaker-fold CV), report mean ± std and apply paired statistical tests for the main pairwise comparisons. (2) Hierarchical ablation: include a joint end-to-end training baseline for the hierarchical model (and/or experiments where Level-1 weights are frozen vs fine-tuned during Level-2 training) to isolate architectural vs training-regime effects. (3) MOUD/text-language controls: report MOUD results using (a) Google-translated transcripts (current), (b) native Spanish embeddings/word vectors and training pipeline, and (c) if available, human-verified transcripts or ASR outputs; explicitly discuss how translation affects modality rankings and cross-dataset transfer. (4) Re-run or re-evaluate prior baselines under the same speaker-disjoint splits and preprocessing where feasible, or clearly annotate comparisons as non-apples-to-apples. (5) Reproducibility appendix: publish exact hyperparameters (LSTM hidden sizes, layers, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, dropout), masking/padding implementation details, random seeds, openSMILE/3D-CNN configuration files, and code/data splits. (6) Broaden metrics: report per-class precision/recall/F1 (and macro/micro F1 or balanced accuracy) especially for multiclass IEMOCAP and imbalanced settings. (7) Applicability clarification: explicitly state the offline assumption for bc-LSTM and, if relevant, add a causal/streaming comparison. Implementing these items will clarify the causal sources of gains and improve reproducibility.
transparency_report: What is transparent in the manuscript: clear motivation and logical framing for temporal context; explicit architectural descriptions (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) and hierarchical vs non-hierarchical fusion; pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and feature-extractor overviews (text-CNN, openSMILE, 3D-CNN) that support partial reproducibility.

What is under-documented: lack of repeated-run statistics, missing full hyperparameter lists (exact learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, early stopping criteria), incomplete masking/padding implementation details, and absence of random-seed disclosure.

Comparative transparency issue: comparisons to prior literature are reported but often under differing evaluation protocols (speaker-overlapping prior splits vs present speaker-disjoint splits) and the paper does not consistently mark these as non-apples-to-apples in tabulated comparisons.

Cross-lingual preprocessing transparency: MOUD used Google Translate for transcripts; authors mention Spanish embeddings improve performance but do not include native-language runs in main results—this creates an explicit transparency gap affecting modality and transfer claims.

Code/data transparency: no public code or split files referenced in the manuscript (per reviewers); releasing code and exact splits would substantially improve transparency and enable independent verification.
epistemic_limits: The reviewers collectively identify several limits to confidence in the manuscript's quantitative generalization claims. First, single-split single-run point estimates without confidence intervals limit inferential strength: reported small-to-moderate gains (especially sub-5% improvements) may not be robust to alternative speaker partitions or random seeds. Second, cross-paper SOTA comparisons are epistemically limited when prior work used different evaluation protocols (speaker-overlap vs speaker-disjoint); such comparisons should be interpreted as indicative rather than conclusive unless baselines are re-run under identical conditions. Third, the hierarchical fusion benefit is epistemically ambiguous because separate Level-1/Level-2 training confounds architecture with training schedule and optimization budget; without joint-training baselines the causal attribution to architecture is uncertain. Fourth, MOUD translation introduces language and preprocessing confounds that limit conclusions about modality robustness and cross-lingual transfer—translation quality and embedding language materially affect textual results. Fifth, bc-LSTM results assume offline availability of future context; conclusions drawn for online/real-time systems do not generalize without further causal-setting experiments. Finally, implementation-level omissions (masking, hyperparameters, seeds) constrain reproducibility and thereby the degree to which independent researchers can verify the reported effects. Collectively these epistemic limits imply that the core qualitative insight (context helps) is plausible within the reported offline protocol, but quantitative effect sizes and cross-dataset generality remain provisional until the above uncertainties are addressed.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes modeling inter-utterance temporal context for utterance-level multimodal (text, audio, visual) sentiment and emotion classification via LSTM-based contextual encoders and compares architectural variants (sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM) and fusion regimes (non-hierarchical concat-then-LSTM vs hierarchical unimodal contextual LSTMs feeding a Level-2 contextual LSTM). Experiments on MOSI, MOUD, and IEMOCAP (speaker-disjoint splits) report consistent within-protocol improvements over a uni-SVM baseline and higher accuracies than cited prior work, with qualitative findings that bc-LSTM and hierarchical fusion often yield better offline accuracy and that text is typically the strongest unimodal signal in-language while visual features show relative robustness under a MOSI→MOUD cross-dataset transfer.
strengths: Clear motivation and formulation: the paper motivates why neighboring utterances can disambiguate sentiment/emotion and maps this to sequence modeling with LSTMs.

Well-specified architectures and ablations: sc-LSTM, h-LSTM, bc-LSTM variants and both hierarchical/non-hierarchical fusion are described with pseudocode and feature-pipeline details (text-CNN, openSMILE, 3D-CNN).

Broad empirical coverage within the chosen protocol: experiments span three public datasets (MOSI, MOUD, IEMOCAP), per-modality analyses, fusion comparisons, and a cross-dataset transfer (MOSI→MOUD), and prioritize speaker-disjoint splits to probe unseen-speaker generalization.
limitations: Statistical robustness missing: results are reported as single-point accuracies on single speaker-disjoint splits with no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or formal statistical tests; many reported gains are small (<5%) and may not be robust to split/seed variability.

Hierarchical fusion training confound: the hierarchical pipeline trains Level-1 unimodal contextual LSTMs and Level-2 sequentially (successive separate training). Without a joint end-to-end baseline or frozen/fine-tune ablations, it is unclear whether gains derive from architecture or from the staged training/regimen and hyperparameter tuning.

Cross-dataset / language preprocessing confound: MOUD textual experiments use Google Translate to English; the authors note Spanish word vectors change results (∼10%), so modality rankings and MOSI→MOUD transfer conclusions are confounded by translation/embedding choices.

Operational applicability of bc-LSTM: reported bc-LSTM advantages assume offline access to future utterances at test time; no experiments or discussion quantify how much of the gain survives in causal/streaming settings.
open_questions: Please provide variability estimates: can the authors re-run key experiments across multiple random speaker-disjoint splits (or k-fold speaker-level CV) and report mean ± std and paired statistical tests comparing hierarchical vs non-hierarchical and bc-LSTM vs sc/h-LSTM?

Can the authors include a joint end-to-end training baseline for the hierarchical architecture (or an ablation where Level-1 is frozen vs fine-tuned during Level-2 training) to disentangle architectural benefits from staged-training effects?

For MOUD cross-lingual results, please report results using native-language (Spanish) embeddings and the untranslated pipeline (or both translated and native runs) so we can assess how much translation noise drives modality and transfer observations.

Please clarify masking/padding and optimization details: exact LSTM hidden sizes, number of layers, learning rate schedule, batch size, number of epochs, early stopping criteria, random seeds, and how masking is implemented across batches (per-batch padding or global) to support reproducibility.
consensus_snapshot: Modeling inter-utterance temporal context with LSTMs plausibly improves utterance-level multimodal classification performance under the paper's offline speaker-disjoint protocol.

Hierarchical fusion (per-modality contextual LSTMs then a Level-2 contextual LSTM) is a coherent architectural proposal and shows reported gains relative to the non-hierarchical concat-then-LSTM baseline in the manuscript's experiments.
bc-LSTM (bidirectional) commonly outperforms unidirectional variants in offline evaluations where future context is available.

Text tends to be the strongest unimodal signal in in-language settings; visual features appear relatively more robust in the single reported MOSI→MOUD transfer, but this depends on preprocessing choices.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude and generality of the reported 5–10% improvement: some reviewers view it as promising but provisional (due to single-split reporting and preprocessing differences), others caution that cross-paper SOTA comparisons are not apples-to-apples without re-running baselines under identical protocols.

Source of hierarchical gains: some interpret improvements as architectural (hierarchical contextual fusion), others suspect they may arise from the staged training regimen, parameter budget, or per-modality tuning.

uncertainty_snapshot: Lack of statistical variance reporting (no CIs or multiple runs) makes the reliability of small numeric gains uncertain.

Comparisons to prior work may be confounded by differing speaker-split protocols (speaker-overlap in prior SOTA) and preprocessing (MOUD translation), limiting the interpretability of cross-paper SOTA claims.
Hierarchical vs non-hierarchical comparison may be confounded by differences in training schedule/optimization; causal attribution to architecture is therefore uncertain.
bc-LSTM benefits are tied to the offline setting; generalization to online/real-time deployments is uncertain without causal-setting experiments.

transparency_notes: The manuscript transparently presents architecture definitions, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and feature-extractor descriptions (text-CNN, openSMILE, 3D-CNN), which aid reproducibility in principle. However, critical reproducibility items are under-documented or missing: no multiple-run statistics or confidence intervals, incomplete hyperparameter lists (exact LSTM sizes, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, early stopping), masking/padding implementation details, and no public code or explicit split files referenced. Comparative tables include prior SOTA numbers but do not consistently annotate when evaluation protocols differ (speaker-overlap vs speaker-disjoint). human_facing_meta_review.comments: Summary: The paper presents a coherent hierarchical contextual-LSTM approach for utterance-level multimodal sentiment and emotion classification, with clear architecture descriptions and empirical evaluations on MOSI, MOUD and IEMOCAP using speaker-disjoint splits. Strengths: Clear motivation for modeling inter-utterance context, detailed architectural variants and ablations, and broad empirical coverage including modality analyses and a cross-dataset transfer experiment. Limitations: 1) No statistical robustness reporting (no CIs/stds or multiple-split runs), 2) Hierarchical fusion is trained successively (not jointly), confounding architecture with training-regime effects, 3) MOUD translation confound (Google Translate) affects modality/transfer conclusions, 4) bc-LSTM assumes offline future-context availability limiting claims for online settings. Open Questions: 1) Can authors provide multi-split mean ± std and statistical tests to establish robustness of reported gains? 2) Can authors add a joint end-to-end hierarchical baseline (and freeze/fine-tune ablations) to isolate architectural benefits from staged training? 3) Please report MOUD results using native-language embeddings/pipeline to quantify translation impact on modality rankings and transfer. 4) Provide full implementation details for masking/padding and all optimizer/training hyperparameters (and random seeds) or release code. Transparency: Pseudocode and feature descriptions aid reproducibility but significant details and multi-run statistics are missing; comparisons to prior SOTA should be annotated where evaluation protocols differ. The core qualitative claim—that temporal contextual modeling helps in the offline speaker-disjoint setting—is supported by within-protocol results, but quantitative magnitudes and cross-dataset generality are provisional until the requested robustness and control experiments are provided.

Please respond and engage, particularly after the authors’ response has been submitted. The goal here is to catch any mistakes, misunderstandings, or violations of the reviewer guidelines. Possible influence of other reviewers. When you see the reviews by the other reviewers, be aware that they may affect your own judgment in several ways because of social psychology effects. If you pointed out a weakness and then saw it also pointed out by someone else, you may feel it is a more severe problem than you originally thought. You may “discard” your own opinion if you see the opinion of someone you believe to be more senior/experienced/famous. If your original opinion was very positive, in the face of a strongly negative review, you may be tempted to “converge to the mean” (or the other way round). Ask yourself if this is really warranted, and whether this may be reflecting some core dispute between approaches/methodologies etc. Strong disagreements may be an indication that the paper is doing something unusual and interesting.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.
